reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Commonest inherited disorder of fatty-acid oxidation, caused by biallelic ACADM variants; the c.985A>G (p.Lys304Glu) allele predominates in populations of northern European ancestry
The defective enzyme cannot dehydrogenate medium-chain (C6-C10) acyl-CoA substrates, so beta-oxidation stalls once glycogen stores are exhausted during fasting or intercurrent illness
Classic decompensation is hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with lethargy, vomiting and encephalopathy, often after a period of poor feeding or a viral illness
Newborn screening detects a characteristic acylcarnitine profile with elevated octanoylcarnitine (C8) and a raised C8:C10 ratio
Urine organic acids during crisis show medium-chain dicarboxylic aciduria with inappropriately low ketones
Cornerstone of management is avoidance of prolonged fasting, an emergency regimen with oral or intravenous glucose during illness, and prompt presentation when unwell
Many diagnosed on screening remain asymptomatic if fasting is avoided, but sudden unexpected death and Reye-like presentations occurred historically before screening
reference.pathophysiology: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase catalyses the first, rate-limiting dehydrogenation step of mitochondrial beta-oxidation for medium-chain fatty acyl-CoA esters. When the enzyme is deficient, fatty acids cannot be fully oxidised to supply acetyl-CoA and hepatic ketone bodies during fasting, so tissues that depend on ketones and fatty-acid-derived energy are compromised and hypoglycaemia develops once hepatic glycogen is depleted. Accumulating medium-chain acyl-CoA intermediates are diverted to carnitine esters and dicarboxylic acids, and the shortage of acetyl-CoA impairs ureagenesis, producing hyperammonaemia in severe crises.
additionalDifferentials: Other fatty-acid oxidation defects (VLCAD, LCHAD/trifunctional protein, SCAD deficiencies)
Carnitine cycle disorders (CPT1, CPT2, translocase, primary carnitine deficiency)
Ketotic hypoglycaemia and glycogen storage disorders
Sepsis or acute viral encephalopathy in an unwell infant
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile by tandem mass spectrometry (elevated C8, raised C8:C10)
Urine organic acids seeking medium-chain dicarboxylic aciduria and hexanoylglycine/suberylglycine
Blood glucose, ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate), ammonia and lactate during acute illness
ACADM molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Enzyme assay in fibroblasts or leucocytes where genotype is inconclusive
redFlags: Reduced consciousness or seizures with documented hypoketotic hypoglycaemia
Vomiting and refusal to feed during intercurrent illness in a known or at-risk infant
Hyperammonaemia or hepatic dysfunction suggesting metabolic decompensation
Apparent life-threatening event or sudden unexpected collapse in a young infant
reference.prognosis: With newborn screening, education on fasting avoidance and a written emergency regimen, the long-term outlook is excellent and most individuals develop normally. Risk of morbidity and death concentrates in the first decompensation, so prevention and early recognition are decisive.
pitfalls: Attributing hypoglycaemia to a simple viral illness and missing the underlying oxidation defect
Expecting ketosis to accompany hypoglycaemia, when the hallmark is that ketones are inappropriately low
Allowing prolonged fasting for procedures or investigations without a glucose-containing infusion
Assuming an asymptomatic screen-detected infant needs no emergency plan
references: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
management: Strict avoidance of prolonged fasting with regular carbohydrate-rich feeds and age-appropriate maximum fasting intervals
Written emergency regimen using oral glucose polymer during intercurrent illness, escalating to intravenous glucose if oral intake fails
During decompensation, intravenous dextrose to reverse hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and suppress lipolysis, with correction of hyperammonaemia
Low threshold for prompt hospital attendance during any febrile or vomiting illness
Avoid medium-chain triglyceride supplements and fat-loading, with metabolic dietitian involvement
Consider L-carnitine supplementation where secondary carnitine depletion is documented
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with sibling testing and newborn-screening cascade
Provide emergency alert documentation identifying the metabolic diagnosis
